abstract: The continuously growing mouse incisor provides a useful model for investigating stem cell niche organization and the MSC-to-TAC transition because it contains spatially distinct mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-enriched and transit-amplifying cell (TAC)-enriched compartments and abundant TAC populations. However, the metabolic programs associated with MSCs and their transition to TACs within the native tissue environment remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated region-resolved transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics with single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize metabolic remodeling associated with the MSC-to-TAC transition in the mouse incisor pulp. We found that the MSC-enriched apical pulp was enriched for molecular features associated with fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body metabolism, whereas the TAC-enriched mitotic pulp showed molecular signatures associated with the tricarboxylic acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and nucleotide biosynthesis. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed lower mRNA-protein concordance in the MSC-enriched apical pulp, consistent with a contribution of post-transcriptional regulation, whereas the TAC-enriched mitotic pulp showed tighter mRNA-protein coupling. Metabolite profiling further showed higher abundance of acyl-carnitines and ketone bodies in the MSC-enriched apical pulp and higher abundance of glutamine, aspartate, and purine intermediates in the TAC-enriched mitotic pulp. Pseudotime analysis suggested coordinated changes in transcriptional programs related to fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, and nucleotide synthesis along an MSC-to-TAC trajectory. Collectively, our study establishes a region-resolved multi-omics atlas of metabolic remodeling associated with the MSC-to-TAC transition in the mouse incisor and provides insights into the metabolic features associated with stem cell activation, progenitor expansion, and tissue homeostasis in the native dental stem cell niche.
